paras: The Union gambling raid killing was the fatal shooting of a Black man named Washington or Columbus Jay by a policeman during a raid on a gambling party in Union, South Carolina, on Saturday night, May 2, 1903. A coroner's jury found that policeman William O'Shields had fired the fatal shot, and he was jailed and tried for murder, but a jury acquitted him in June after deliberating seven minutes. The case drew most comment for the acquittal, which the Abbeville Press and Banner headlined "Acquitted, of Course."

According to the Union Times, the dead man had come to Union from Aiken County about two weeks earlier and was employed at Buffalo. A Union special in the Kingstree County Record said most of the men at the game had been brought from Georgia to work at Buffalo.

On Saturday night policemen Johnson, Johns and O'Shields raided a cabin opposite the Union Mills warehouse where Black men were gambling; the Ledger's correspondent called it the house of Elmira Minter, a Black woman. One officer went inside while two stayed out, and when he entered the lights were blown out and the men scattered. In the Ledger's version the men ran out the other door and "the police began shooting," hitting two of them.

Jay was shot in the back as he ran, the ball ranging upward through his body, and he died on Sunday. A second man was shot in the foot, according to the County Record, whose correspondent placed the fatal wound in the bowels. Jay told Sergeant Austelle he did not know who shot him, but a Black witness, Arthur Sortar, said he saw O'Shields fire five times.

At Coroner Gregory's inquest, the Union Times reported, it was shown that one man did all the shooting, and the jury found Jay died "at the hands of Wm. O'Shields." The County Record's correspondent wrote that witnesses at the inquest said the police had killed him, while a policeman said he had found a man shot but did not know who shot him. O'Shields was jailed, and on Wednesday, May 13, Judge Townsend refused him bail, leaving him in jail until the next term of court.

At that term O'Shields was tried for murder in Union and acquitted on Monday, June 15. The Abbeville Press and Banner reported that the jury took only seven minutes and that the testimony was conflicting. O'Shields stayed on the force: on June 20, on duty at a mill ball game, he split the ear of Bob Horn, the mill's assistant boss, with his club.

The killing was reported only in South Carolina weeklies, first as one-sentence items in state news columns. The Abbeville Press and Banner said two men were shot "in attempting to escape from the police," and the Newberry Herald and News and the Lexington Dispatch printed a near-identical line about a man killed by a raiding officer. The Union Times headed its local report "Negro Killed by Policeman" and referred to the officers as "Messrs." and to the accused as "Mr. O'Shields," while giving the dead man no honorific. The Lancaster Ledger's dispatch, headed "Killed by a Police Officer," was the only report to name the house's occupant or to print a Black eyewitness's account.

The sharpest comment came after the trial, when the Abbeville Press and Banner, under the headline "Acquitted, of Course," wrote that the policeman "had done nothing worse than shooting a negro in the back." The Newberry Herald and News, reporting the same verdict, instead adopted the officers' version, describing Jay as one of a crowd of gamblers who "resisted" arrest. When O'Shields clubbed Horn, a Carolina Spartan item reprinted in the Union Times introduced him as the policeman tried "for killing a negro and came clear."

The papers disagreed on the dead man's first name: the Union Times called him Washington Jay, while the Lancaster Ledger and the Newberry Herald and News called him Columbus Jay. Every account of the night describes flight, but the Newberry paper's post-trial item says the men "resisted." On who fired, the coroner's jury and Sortar named O'Shields; only a policeman and the dying man said the shooter was unknown.

bases: A policeman on a raid shot a fleeing Black man in the back and a coroner's jury named him as the killer (A2, A4); he was tried for murder and acquitted (A8, A9).

The local Union Times (A2), a Union dispatch to the Lancaster Ledger (A4) and a Union special in the County Record (A6) independently agree that police raiding a gambling party shot and killed a Black man, and two papers report the trial and acquittal (A8, A9).

framing.detail: May state-news columns gave one sentence: gamblers shot 'in attempting to escape from the police' or a man 'caught in a gambling den' killed by a raiding officer.
The Union Times headed it 'Negro Killed by Policeman' and called the officers 'Messrs.' and the accused 'Mr. O'Shields'.
The Abbeville Press and Banner's 'Acquitted, of Course' said sarcastically that the policeman 'had done nothing worse than shooting a negro in the back.'
The Newberry Herald and News reported the acquittal while describing the gamblers as having 'resisted' arrest, the officers' version.

conflicts.note: The local Union Times uses Washington twice; the Union dispatch and the Newberry trial item use Columbus. Neither can be preferred on these texts.

info: Saturday night, 1903-05-02; the County Record alone says Sunday night
A cabin on the bluff opposite the Union Mills warehouse, behind the old Moore residence (Union Times); the house of Elmira Minter, a Black woman (Lancaster Ledger); Union, S.C.
Washington Jay (Union Times) or Columbus Jay (Lancaster Ledger, Newberry Herald and News), a Black man from Aiken County employed at Buffalo; a second Black man, unnamed, shot in the foot
Gambling; the men were described as fleeing the raid (A1, A2, A4), and the Newberry Herald and News later said they 'resisted' arrest (A9)
Policeman William (Wm., Bill) O'Shields, named by the coroner's jury and an eyewitness; raid party also included policemen Johnson and Johns
Acquitted of murder (Monday before the June 17 Abbeville issue); O'Shields was back on police duty by June 20
